title: Navigating scarcity: sustainable supply network archetypes for water stress
authors: Ekaterina Yatskovskaya; Naoum Tsolakis; Jagjit Singh Srai
affiliations: IESEG School of Management – Campus de Paris , ,; Department of Engineering, Institute for Manufacturing, University of Cambridge , ,; Department of Supply Chain Management, School of Economics and Business Administration, International Hellenic University , ,
abstract: Purpose This study examines how firms configure sustainable supply networks (SNs) under water scarcity. It explains how water dependence shapes capability-configuration bundles and introduces transformational capability as the capacity to orchestrate capabilities for architecture-level redesign of SNs. Design/methodology/approach An abductive multiple-case study compares 13 multinational manufacturers across four sectors. Evidence from 23 interviews, site observations and secondary sources was analysed using Gioia-inspired coding and cross-case pattern matching. Findings Three contingent sustainable SN archetypes emerge: (1) “Stable”, (2) “Continuous Improvement”; and (3) “Progressive”. They differ in the scope of water dependence, the breadth of capabilities and the scope for reconfiguration. Static capabilities support routine monitoring and efficiency; dynamic capabilities renew existing processes and relationships; transformational capabilities orchestrate combinations of the five capability clusters to alter product and material choices, sourcing, governance, location, infrastructure or network structure. This is most evident in the “Progressive Sustainable SN” archetype. Research limitations/implications The qualitative study focuses on multinational manufacturers. Future research in other sectors, such as energy, should test the archetypes and transitions across smaller firms, services and other contexts of natural resource scarcity. Practical implications Managers can diagnose water dependence, distinguish incremental adaptation from transformational reconfiguration and align capability investments with changes across operations, sourcing, products, governance and network design. Social implications The developed framework can inform decisions on industrial location, catchment stewardship and shared water resilience. Originality/value The study advances a contingency-informed SN configuration perspective through a nested framework of sustainable SN archetypes. The archetypes are theorised as distinct configuration–capability combinations rather than as descriptive groupings of known adaptation practices. It establishes transformational capability as a distinct sustainable SN capability, rather than a synonym for dynamic capability, and explains when capabilities trigger architecture-level redesign under water scarcity.

title: “The Minimum Wage Is the Maximum Wage”: How Goal Replacement Perpetuates Means–Ends Decoupling
affiliations: Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg
abstract: This research examines how organizations contribute to the perpetuation of means–ends decoupling (MED) within issue-based fields organized around societal problems, under conditions of heightened field scrutiny. In such settings, organizations often profess commitment to field goals and visibly comply with institutionally prescribed practices to satisfy monitoring, reporting, and public evaluation requirements. However, many adopted goals remain underachieved, raising questions about how compliance without progress endures and how claims of commitment remain credible under transparency regimes intended to spur substantive goal pursuit. Our data came from 75 interviews with 68 brands, suppliers, and third-party organizations pursuing worker well-being in global fashion supply chains. We unveil auditability-based goal replacement as an organizational-level mechanism through which actors rhetorically foreground compliance as public evidence of commitment while narrowing internal goal pursuit to auditable thresholds that serve their core goals, thereby allowing shortfalls to persist. Self-silencing about this substitution and the instrumentalizing of shortfalls close the configuration into a self-reinforcing loop. The study advances MED scholarship by (i) showing how organizations leverage field conditions and appropriate the existing scrutiny infrastructures to advance their core goals while reproducing the means–ends gap, (ii) problematizing the authenticity of commitment claims, and (iii) explaining how goal-ineffective compliance prevails as a credible substitute for adopted goals. It also extends research on organizational responses to institutional complexity and calls for greater attention to institutional impact—that is, the realized advancement of the societal aim an institution emerged to address.

title: Human Development and the Architecture of Everyday Worry: Latent Worry Profiles in the World Risk Poll
affiliations: Centre for Behavioural and Implementation Science Interventions (BISI), Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine National University of Singapore Singapore Singapore; Department of Sociology and Social Research University of Trento Trento Italy
abstract: ABSTRACT Whether public concern about risk rises or falls with national development has been debated for three decades, but the debate has compared countries hazard by hazard, asking how much people worry rather than how worry is organized. We provide a person‐centered analysis of everyday worry at global scale, applying latent class analysis to the six‐hazard worry battery of the Lloyd's Register Foundation World Risk Poll and linking profiles to the Human Development Index (HDI) in 140 countries (; 2023 wave), with the 2021 wave (; 119 countries) as an independent replication. Four worry profiles replicate almost exactly across waves, including a configurationally distinct secure‐basics profile (15% of respondents) combining low worry about food and water with high worry about crime, severe weather, and traffic. Profile prevalence is consistent with the ordered sequence predicted by a need‐priority account of worry allocation: pervasive worry falls from 33% to 13% between low‐ and very‐high‐HDI countries, low worry nearly doubles, and the secure‐basics profile holds steady across low‐ and medium‐HDI countries before declining at higher development. Traffic accidents are the most intense worry in every tier below very high HDI. These gradients persist after adjustment for self‐reported recent harm and demographic composition and are only partly accounted for by the objective hazard environment, though the cross‐sectional design cannot separate development from macroregional clustering. Development is associated with the composition of worry, not only its overall level; risk communication may be better matched to a country's worry architecture than to a single global template.

title: Comparing Like With Like in Biological Invasion Risk Analysis
affiliations: Department of Ecology and Vertebrate Zoology Faculty of Biology and Environmental Protection University of Lodz Lodz Poland
abstract: ABSTRACT Biological invasion decision‐support methods are often compared under broad labels such as “risk assessment,” even when they perform different functions. This Perspective argues that functional commensurability must be established before methods are compared. In biological invasion risk analysis, screening serves an initial risk identification function, flagging extant or horizon non‐native species within a defined risk assessment area for prevention, surveillance, or more detailed evaluation. Comprehensive risk assessment examines entry or introduction, establishment, spread, and their ecological, economic, and socio‐cultural consequences in greater detail. Risk management integrates risk with feasibility, cost, effectiveness, legal constraints, and stakeholder values. Impact classification and post‐establishment population prioritization may contribute to these functions without being equivalent to them. Published comparisons show how conflating such functions can create false equivalence. The emerging Dispersal‐Origin‐Status‐Impact (DOSI) literature provides an illustrative example through its comparisons with applications of the globally implemented Invasiveness Screening Kit (ISK) decision‐support tools: population status and management priority are not the same quantities as prospective invasion risk screening, and species‐based screening does not imply coarse spatial resolution. Forty‐five peer‐reviewed ISK‐family studies report local or subnational screenings, including spatial resolutions comparable with or finer than DOSI applications. Valid comparisons require a shared decision objective, explicit spatial and temporal boundaries, independent evaluation evidence, and assessment of uncertainty and the consequences of error. These requirements permit methods to be evaluated for a common use, or combined within adaptive management, without treating disagreement between unlike outputs as evidence of superior performance.

title: Synthesizing Information-Driven Insider Trade Signals
authors: Jens Heckmann; Heiko Jacobs; Patrick Schwarz
affiliations: University of Duisburg-Essen; University of Liège HEC Liège
abstract: Abstract We propose a novel approach to synthesize presumably information-driven insider trading signals for the cross section of stocks. We find that the resulting straightforward composite strategy can often forecast returns in a global sample. This predictability is strongest in equal-weighted portfolios, short holding periods, and insider-buying signals, and it improves further with global diversification. Cross-country analysis reveals that varying insider trading restrictions between countries have limited explanatory power for the performance of the composite strategy. Overall, the results are consistent with a short-term informational advantage of insiders, which might be due to the skillful interpretation of non-private news.

title: Beyond the Battlefield: Localized Civilian Clashes and Political Attitudes in Violent Conflict
authors: Carly Wayne; Sivan Hirsch-Hoefler; Masanori Kikuchi; Daphna Canetti
affiliations: Washington University in St Louis; Reichman University; University of Haifa
abstract: Abstract In protracted conflicts, civilians frequently encounter low-level, hostile actions from adversary civilians in nearby communities, yet the political consequences of these events remain understudied. We investigate this question in the Israeli–Palestinian context, examining how community-level exposure to hostile actions by Israeli settlers shapes Palestinian political attitudes in the West Bank. Leveraging a novel data set containing thousands of geo-coded conflict events from 2010 to 2020 paired with forty-six Palestinian public opinion polls in the West Bank, we find that district-level increases in settler hostilities are significantly associated with heightened political militancy among local Palestinians, associations that are larger and more robust than those from local Israeli military actions. A second empirical strategy examining changes in Palestinian attitudes before and after the establishment of nearby settler outposts reveals that this form of civilian land expropriation likewise leads to modest increases in political militancy among Palestinians in proximate towns. These findings highlight the distinct political impact of localized, low-level civilian actions and territorial expropriation—central but often overlooked features of sectarian territorial conflicts—offering insights for territorial and ethnic disputes globally.

title: Geoengineering, Moral Hazard, and Disrespect
affiliations: University of Reading
abstract: Abstract Scientists and policy makers are increasingly exploring solar geoengineering as a tool for combatting anthropogenic climate change. Yet these technologies have drawn intense ethical criticism. One of the most influential critiques – the ‘moral hazard’ objection – holds that pursuing solar geoengineering risks undercutting mitigation efforts; and that, as a result, governments should halt the development of solar geoengineering. This paper argues that the moral hazard objection faces a dilemma: either the proposed solution to the moral hazard effect (that is, stifling geoengineering) is unnecessary, or it expresses a morally troubling form of disrespect. Articulating this dilemma serves three purposes. It shows, first, that the moral hazard objection is substantially more difficult to vindicate than it initially appears. Second, it clarifies what would need to be shown, empirically, to overcome this ethical hurdle. Finally, and crucially, it sheds light, more broadly, on what it means to respect people’s agency when designing and implementing public policies.

title: When Politics Enters the Waiting Room: Far-Right Electoral Victories Exacerbate Discrimination in Access to Healthcare
authors: MERLIN SCHAEFFER; ALESSIO ROMARRI; DINA ROSENBERG; KRZYSZTOF KRAKOWSKI
affiliations: University of Copenhagen; Autonomous University of Barcelona; Rowan University; Collegio Carlo Alberto
abstract: Abstract Far-right political shifts have been linked to increased racism, raising concerns about their impact on minority access to public services. This study investigates whether far-right electoral victories encourage discrimination by street-level bureaucrats, who are expected to act impartially. We conducted a nested research design in Italy, combining a field-experimental audit with a regression discontinuity design focused on municipalities near the electoral threshold for far-right mayors. Research assistants with native-Italian and West-African accents contacted municipal healthcare offices to request registration with a general medical practitioner. Compared to native-Italian callers, those with West-African accents faced significantly higher rates of scrutiny and dismissive responses. Leveraging close elections, we find that this disparity was exacerbated in municipalities where far-right candidates narrowly won. These findings demonstrate that far-right electoral success can undermine impartiality and equal access to essential services.

title: Conceptual search: A generative view of entrepreneurial imagination
affiliations: Ross School of Business University of Michigan Ann Arbor Michigan USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs cannot pursue ventures they never imagine. This article develops a generative view of entrepreneurial imagination as the construction of an evolving candidate set through generation, provisional evaluation, and revision. Conceptual search represents venture concepts as text, transforms them through interpretable operations, and compares their promise. A large language model prototype demonstrates complementary modes: local refinement lifts a concept from sixteenth to third among 30 ventures under a validated evaluator, while global recombination reaches distant possibilities that refinement makes competitive. The framework shows how search architecture determines what enters, survives, and develops, and how AI may broaden imagination within firms while producing correlated imagination across firms. By making imagination programmable, auditable, and experimentally tractable, conceptual search opens a research program on how entrepreneurial possibilities are constructed. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs can pursue only the ventures they imagine, and valuable ideas routinely go unbuilt because nobody thinks of them. AI makes imagining cheap: it can draft, critique, and rewrite venture concepts in seconds, so developing ideas becomes a process that can be designed, run, and audited. I demonstrate a system that evolves real venture concepts: step‐by‐step refinement lifted a middling concept to third place among 30 real ventures, as ranked by an AI judge shown to predict fundraising, while recombining distant ideas created novel concepts that refinement made competitive. The entrepreneur's job shifts from generating a few ideas to governing many: choosing what to search, keep, and test in the market. One caution: rivals using the same AI will imagine similar ventures; advantage comes from proprietary problems, data, and evidence.

title: All in order? Older female influencers’ displays of ageing on social media
authors: Malene Gram; Benedetta Cappellini; Stephanie O’Donohoe; Vicki Harman
affiliations: Aalborg University, Denmark; Durham University, UK; University of Edinburgh, UK; University of Reading, UK
abstract: Drawing on qualitative interviews in the UK and Denmark, we analyse how female influencers aged 50+ discuss the presentation of their bodies on Instagram. We advance Julia Twigg’s theorising of age ordering – body and dress norms devaluing older women – and Janet Finch’s concept of display by applying these to influencer culture in digital consumer society. Our findings illuminate participants’ desire to share positive experiences of being at the time of life they are, within the bodies that they are, and the normative constraints they experience on their dress and bodily display. We identify three non-exclusive display positions: ordering (accepting norms around older female bodies), reordering (negotiating these norms by striving for a youthful look), and disordering (challenging those norms). We suggest that reordering is the new ordering but find positions of disordering in all age groups, and examine how the digital and commercial context influences these displays of ageing.

title: Craft and Industrialization: Uncovering the Plasticity and Frontier of Craft
affiliations: Tampere University; University of Helsinki
abstract: Abstract Craft as an approach to work has been proposed as an alternative to industrial mass production. While industrialization has led to the replacement of craft logic with industrial logic to create uniformity and scale operations, the role of craft in industrialization remains ambiguous. Building on the analysis of engineering work performed at an R&D laboratory in the pulp and paper industry, we explore how and why craft enables industrialization. Our findings reveal how elements of craft manifest in engineering work by helping to transform ideas into useful objects, balancing scientific accuracy with practical usefulness, and fostering a sense of community and identity within the engineering field. These findings point to the plasticity of craft logic , suggesting that elements of craft can be transferred into new contexts and reinterpreted to address new objectives. Considering that these activities took place in an R&D laboratory that drove industrialization, they also reveal the existence of a craft frontier that escapes standardization by providing a context for crafting candidates for future standards. Craft frontier enables the coexistence of craft and industrial logics, where craft can contribute to industrialization by establishing foundations for managerial control without being absorbed into it.

title: The Many Faces of Process Complexity
authors: Sandro Franzoi; Thomas Grisold; Nicholas Berente; Jan vom Brocke
affiliations: University of Münster; Vienna University of Economics and Business; University of Notre Dame
abstract: Process complexity is a widely used concept for analyzing and improving socio-technical processes, but the term is applied in inconsistent ways, and its conceptualizations and operationalizations are often ambiguous. As a result, the same process can appear highly complex under one operationalization and comparatively simple under another, fragmenting insights across research streams. To map and structure the various approaches to process complexity, we conduct a scoping review across three domains in which process complexity has been studied: information systems, organization science, and computer science. We identify 21 distinct operationalizations of process complexity and organize them along six levels of analysis (process, between-sequence, sequence, partial pattern, action pair, and single action). By expressing these operationalizations in a unified notation and characterizing each by its underlying computation and level of analysis, we provide a means for measuring, relating, and comparing different forms of process complexity. This multi-level understanding allows researchers to investigate trade-offs, tipping points, and optimal degrees of complexity across processes. We conclude with a reflection on the implications for information systems research and practice.

title: The threat‐enhancing effect of authoritarian power sharing
affiliations: Associate Professor, Department of Political Science Emory University Atlanta Georgia USA
abstract: Abstract Power‐sharing deals can potentially solve the autocrat's commitment problem, yet often fail to prevent conflict. This article develops a dynamic model to examine a largely overlooked friction: Sharing power within an authoritarian regime bolsters the opposition's coercive capabilities. The resultant threat‐enhancing effect creates two distinct commitment problems for the opposition, which determine if and when power sharing occurs. First, the opposition cannot commit to refrain from leveraging its enhanced threat. The ruler prefers to incur a revolt than peacefully share power if the threat‐enhancing effect is large. Second, the threat‐enhancing effect tempts the opposition to wait for a future power‐sharing deal, which undercuts the opposition's commitment to revolt today. New dynamic implications arise: delayed power sharing, conflict, or an increased willingness for the ruler to share power are all possible. Scrutinizing the opposition's limited commitment ability contrasts with the predominant existing focus on the autocrat's commitment problem.
